name: Chewmaxxing

lead: Chewmaxxing is the practice of chewing tough foods or gum in large amounts to build the masseter and temporalis muscles. Practitioners hope the added muscle gives a squarer jaw angle and a more sculpted lower face.

The masseter is a muscle that responds to heavy use: habitual clenching, grinding or frequent gum chewing can enlarge it, and clinicians treat the opposite problem, an overly bulky jaw, in cosmetic practices. Forum members cite this as the basis for deliberately training the jaw; published trials of chewing for facial aesthetics are not available.

paras: People typically chew sugar-free gum or firm, fibrous foods for set periods each day, sometimes using dedicated jaw trainers, and combine it with leanness and good posture. Reports of timelines vary by individual and are anecdotal.

Reported downsides include jaw-joint (TMJ) discomfort, headaches, muscle soreness, tooth wear and uneven masseter growth. Dental and medical sources note that chronic clenching is associated with these problems.

chain: Wider, more defined lower face and jaw angle
angle.text: Practitioners chew gum or firm foods to thicken the masseters, aiming for a squarer jaw and fuller lower face. The look depends on the starting bone structure and on body fat, which forum members often pair it with reducing.

lead: Chewmaxxing is a looksmaxxing practice in which people chew gum or hard foods heavily in order to enlarge the masseter and, in some versions, the temporalis muscles. The goal is a stronger-looking jaw angle and fuller lower face, which proponents describe as a natural alternative to jaw fillers or implants.[1]

The idea rests on a real property of the masseter: it can enlarge with frequent use. Habitual clenching, grinding or frequent gum chewing are described as causes of masseter hypertrophy, which can change the shape of the face.[2] A review quoted on looksmax.org notes that chronic clenching can give the face a masculine, square look.[1]

Chewmaxxing sits in the softmaxxing end of looksmaxxing alongside practices such as mewing, which also targets the jaw and lower face through everyday habits rather than procedures.[3][4] Forum discussion covers chewing gum, tougher foods, and whether muscle growth can help balance features such as a narrow forehead.[5][6]

Published research on the underlying tissue is mostly clinical: the masseter's enlargement from clenching, grinding and gum chewing is described in medical references, and botulinum toxin injections into the masseter and temporalis are used to slim an enlarged lower face or treat bruxism.[2][7] No formal trials of chewing programs for facial appearance are known.

paras: Chewmaxxing centres on the masseter, the main muscle that closes the jaw. It is a thick, roughly quadrilateral muscle with superficial, deep and coronoid parts, running from the cheekbone area to the angle and side of the lower jaw, and it is supplied by the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve.[2] Because it sits at the jaw angle, its bulk contributes to the width of the lower face.[2]

Community posts describe the enlarged masseter as "natural fillers" that can mimic the effect of wraparound jaw implants.[1] Others use the term for building the temporalis to fill out the sides of the head.[5] Practitioners usually describe the method in general terms: regular, sustained chewing of gum or tough, fibrous foods, sometimes with dedicated jaw-trainer devices, alongside a lean physique.[6]

The masseter elevates the mandible to close the jaw, and its superficial fibres can also protrude it.[2] Wikipedia notes that habitual clenching or grinding of the teeth, and constant gum chewing, can enlarge the muscle; the enlargement is described as soft and painless, usually on both sides but sometimes on one.[2] The same page says it can cause facial asymmetry and may be mistaken for salivary-gland disease, dental infection or tumours.[2]

Chewmaxxing proponents reason from this to deliberate loading: if habitual use thickens the muscle, scheduled use should do the same, with the visible result depending on where the muscle inserts and how much soft tissue lies over it.[1] The dermatology review quoted on looksmax.org states that chronic clenching leads to masseter and temporalis hypertrophy that gives the face a masculine, square appearance, and that patients present to cosmetic practices wanting a slimmer, softer face.[1]

Looksmaxxing emerged in the 2010s on incel and manosphere forums and spread to TikTok in the early 2020s, with jaw-focused habits such as mewing among its low-intensity or softmaxxing practices.[3] Mewing, named after British orthodontist John Mew, saw rising search interest from January 2019 according to Google Trends, which brought jaw-and-face habit training into wider view.[4] Chewmaxxing threads on looksmax.org date from at least 2020, with posts titled around a "chewmaxxing pill" and "god tier masseters".[1][8][6]
The idea of chewing for jaw strength is older than the forums: William Semple's 1869 gum patent described a gum intended to clean the teeth and strengthen the jaw.[9]

Proponents argue that moderate masseter growth improves the jaw angle and facial definition, and some point to a person who chews gum and is considered attractive as an example, while others in the same thread ask what it means if an unattractive person chews gum.[8] Some threads discuss whether it can balance a narrow forehead; replies there suggested hairstyles and weight loss as alternatives.[5] Posters also say that the effect is best with favourable bone insertions, and that very large masseters were reduced by treatment in the extreme examples they cite.[1]

Wikipedia describes masseter hypertrophy from frequent gum chewing and bruxism as potentially uneven and sometimes associated with temporomandibular joint problems.[2] Dermatology literature on bruxism describes masseter and temporalis enlargement and cosmetic options to slim the lower face.[1]

On the gum itself, Wikipedia's chewing gum article reports reduced cavities and plaque with xylitol-sweetened gum, and notes that large amounts of sorbitol-containing gum may cause gas or diarrhoea.[9] A 2009 study cited there had 35 adults chew gum for 10 to 15 minutes around meals for four weeks after orthodontic treatment; the article does not report jaw-size outcomes.[9]

Regarding the wider category of jaw-and-face habits, the American Association of Orthodontists has said there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw, and most orthodontists do not regard it as an alternative to jaw surgery.[4]

Bruxism, the clenching and grinding that enlarges the masseter, is associated with jaw-muscle pain and fatigue, temple headaches, tooth wear, fractures and damage to dental work, and temporomandibular joint pain and clicking.[7] Treatments for the resulting problems include habit reversal, night splints and botulinum toxin injected into the masseter and temporalis, whose effects typically last about three months.[7]
Forum members also report that overly large masseters can widen the face more than intended.[1] Heavy chewing is associated by clinicians with jaw soreness and enlargement that can be asymmetric.[2]

Related jaw and lower-face practices include mewing (tongue posture), jaw trainers, masseter botulinum treatment for those who want a slimmer face, and body-fat reduction to reveal jawline definition.[4][7][5]
